screens.title: Setting Up Your Java Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome — in this lesson you will build the toolkit you need to write and run Java programs. We begin by installing a Java Development Kit, then configuring two system variables so the compiler and runtime are available from any terminal. You will learn the difference between the developer toolkit (the JDK), the runtime used to execute programs (the JRE), and the abstract executor that runs Java bytecode (the JVM). After verifying your installation, you'll set up a modern IDE so editing, compiling, and debugging are fast and visual. We will also write and run a simple greeting program both from the command line and inside the IDE, and highlight a few common mistakes that beginners make, such as missing semicolons and incorrect main signatures. By the end of this chapter you will have a working Java toolchain and a repeatable setup routine you can use on Windows or Mac O S. Think of this as preparing your developer kitchen: once your tools are organized, learning Object-Oriented Programming becomes practical and enjoyable. Ready to get your workspace ready?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will confidently install the Java Development Kit and configure the environment so Java commands are available from your terminal. You will be able to explain the roles of the JDK, JRE, and JVM and why each matters when developing or running Java applications. You will set up a modern IDE—recommended is IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition—create a new Java project, select the correct project SDK, and understand how the IDE streamlines compilation and debugging. Finally, you will write, compile, and run a simple program both on the command line and inside the IDE, and you will know how to interpret and fix two common errors: a missing semicolon and an incorrect main method signature. Each objective combines a practical action and a reason why it helps your learning, so you leave with a repeatable routine rather than a one-off setup. These skills remove environment friction and let you focus on learning Java language features and object-oriented design.

screens.title: JDK, JRE, and JVM: Roles and relationships
screens.narratorSegment: Let's make the trio of Java components clear and memorable. The Java Development Kit, or JDK, is the full developer toolkit: it contains the Java compiler, development tools, and the Java Runtime Environment. The JRE provides the environment to run Java applications; it bundles a JVM implementation and the core class libraries. The Java Virtual Machine is the abstract machine that executes Java bytecode and provides platform independence. A useful way to think about this is nested boxes: the JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM. When you develop code you need the JDK because only it includes the compiler that turns human-readable Java files into bytecode. If you only want to run already-compiled programs, the JRE is sufficient. An example: you write HelloWorld. java and run the compiler in the JDK to produce HelloWorld. class. That class file can be executed by any JVM on any platform. A common misconception is thinking the JVM compiles source code — it does not. Compilation is a separate step handled by the compiler in the JDK. Remember: compile with the JDK, run with a JVM inside the JRE. How does that separation affect where you install components on a shared machine?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › JDK, JRE, JVM
Definition and nested metaphor
Think of three nested boxes: JDK (outer) contains the JRE, which contains the JVM. Each layer adds responsibility: compiling, supplying libraries, and executing bytecode.
JDK
Includes the compiler and developer tools to create Java applications.
JRE
Contains the JVM and core libraries needed to run Java programs.
JVM
The software executor that runs Java bytecode on your machine.
Concrete example
You write HelloWorld.java and run the compiler that comes with the JDK to produce HelloWorld.class. The JVM inside the JRE reads and executes that class file. The same HelloWorld.class can run on different platforms that provide a compatible JVM.
Common misconception

The JVM does not compile source code. Compilation to bytecode is performed by the JDK's compiler.

Key takeaway

Install the JDK for development; the JRE and JVM handle execution and portability.

screens.title: Compile and run pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the compile-and-run pipeline helps demystify what happens when you build and execute Java code. The process starts with a source file, typically named with a public class that matches the filename. You run the Java compiler, called javac, which reads. java files and produces. class files containing Java bytecode. Bytecode is not platform machine code; it is an intermediate representation that the JVM interprets or just-in-time compiles to native instructions. When you use the java command to run a program, the JVM loads the class files, verifies their structure, links necessary classes, and executes the entry point method. A concrete example: saving HelloWorld. java, running javac HelloWorld. java creates HelloWorld. class, and running java HelloWorld launches the JVM which looks for the main method and begins execution. A common error to watch for is a filename that does not match the public class name; the compiler will refuse to produce correct class files in that case. Another misconception is thinking java runs source files directly — it runs bytecode only. Keep this pipeline in mind when troubleshooting compilation or runtime failures.

keyIdea.title: Pipeline clarity
keyIdea.text: Source files -> javac -> class files (bytecode) -> java -> JVM executes. Filename and class name must match for public classes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Compile & Run
Step-by-step
1
Write source
Create HelloWorld.java with a public class matching the filename.
2
Compile
Run javac HelloWorld.java to produce HelloWorld.class (bytecode).
3
Run
Execute java HelloWorld. The JVM loads and runs the bytecode, starting at main.
Example

javac HelloWorld.java → HelloWorld.class. Then java HelloWorld launches the JVM to execute the class file.

Troubleshooting notes
  • Filename mismatch: public class name must match the file name exactly, including case.
  • Attempting to run source directly: java expects class names, not source filenames.
  • Path issues: if javac or java are not found, PATH or JAVA_HOME are not configured correctly.
Common mistake

Expecting the JVM to compile source. Compilation is explicit and done by the JDK's compiler.

screens.title: Installing the JDK: key decisions
screens.narratorSegment: Installing the Java Development Kit is straightforward, but there are choices to make. The chapter mentions two common distribution sources: vendor-provided builds and open-source builds. For development, pick the latest stable JDK that matches the course expectations. On Windows, run the installer and note the installation directory; on Mac O S, use the provided package installer and observe the Home path format. After installation, you must configure environment variables so commands work in new terminals. Setting JAVA_HOME to the JDK installation path and adding the JDK bin directory to PATH are the two essential steps. A concrete example: on Windows you might set JAVA_HOME to C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-17 and add %JAVA_HOME%\bin to PATH; on Mac O S you set JAVA_HOME to the JDK home folder and add its bin to PATH. A common misconception is that downloading the JDK is sufficient; without updating PATH or restarting the terminal, commands still won’t be found. Always open a fresh terminal after installation and verify with java -version and javac -version to confirm success. Installing the JDK: key decisions means download a stable jdk, then set java_home and add the jdk bin directory to path so java and javac are available system-wide.. In practical terms, choose a jdk distribution and follow the platform installation steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Install JDK
Platform steps (overview)
Windows: Run installer, note install path, set JAVA_HOME to the JDK folder, add %JAVA_HOME%\bin to PATH, then open a new terminal.
macOS: Install package, use the JDK home path format, set JAVA_HOME accordingly, and add the JDK bin to PATH before verifying.
Tip

Choose a stable LTS or course-specified JDK version. Keep track of the installation path for configuring environment variables.

Example values
Windows example: JAVA_HOME = C:\\Program Files\\Java\\jdk-17 and add %JAVA_HOME%\\bin to PATH.
macOS example: JAVA_HOME = /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/jdk-17.jdk/Contents/Home and add the bin directory to PATH.
Common mistake

Not restarting the terminal after updating PATH. Changes apply only to new sessions.

screens.title: Verifying your installation
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the simplest but most important step after installation. Open a new terminal window and run two commands: one to check the runtime and one to check the compiler. The commands are java -version and javac -version. If both return the same vendor and version number, your environment variables and PATH are correctly configured. If java returns a version but javac is not found, it means the runtime is available but the compiler path is missing — typically PATH lacks the JDK bin directory. Conversely, if neither command is found, the installation may have failed or PATH was not updated at all. As a concrete example, successful output will report a version string such as the installed JDK version. When troubleshooting, double-check the JAVA_HOME value and that PATH includes the bin folder, then restart the terminal and try again. A misconception to avoid is thinking a GUI installer finishes all configuration; some installers require manual PATH edits. Confirming both commands works before moving to the IDE saves time and confusion. Verifying your installation means run java -version and javac -version in a fresh terminal. matching versions confirm a correct jdk installation and path setup.. In practical terms, commands to check java and javac and how to interpret results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Verify Install
Terminal checks
$ java -version
java version "17.0.x"  
$ javac -version
javac 17.0.x
Matching version numbers indicate both runtime and compiler are from the same JDK installation.
Troubleshoot
  • If javac is not found, add the JDK bin to PATH or set JAVA_HOME correctly.
  • Restart the terminal to apply environment variable changes before re-running checks.
  • Confirm you edited system-wide variables or user profile for persistent access.

screens.title: Why use an IDE: IntelliJ or Eclipse
screens.narratorSegment: Modern IDEs like IntelliJ IDEA or Eclipse accelerate development by providing powerful editing, project management, and debugging features. Rather than typing source in a plain text editor and switching to the terminal for compilation, an IDE gives you intelligent code completion, real-time syntax and type checking, quick navigation between classes, and integrated run and debug controls. For example, IntelliJ can detect a missing semicolon and highlight the exact location before you attempt to compile. The IDE also manages a project SDK, ensuring consistent use of the correct JDK for building and running. For beginners, the most helpful benefits are immediate feedback on syntax, inline hints for method signatures, and a one-click run action that compiles and launches your program. A common misconception is that IDEs hide what's happening under the hood; in reality, they surface compiler errors and stack traces, helping you learn diagnostics. Use the IDE to speed iterative edits, but understand the underlying compile-run pipeline so you can work outside the IDE when necessary. Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › IDEs
IDE features that help learners
  • Intelligent code completion and inline error highlights.
  • Integrated run and debug tools with stack traces and breakpoints.
  • Project management and automatic compilation on run.
Concrete example

IntelliJ highlights a missing semicolon instantly and offers quick-fix suggestions, speeding up the edit-compile cycle.

Selecting the Project SDK
When creating a new Java project, choose the installed JDK as the Project SDK. This ensures the IDE compiles and runs code using the same JDK you verified earlier.
Key takeaway

screens.title: Create a new Java project in IntelliJ
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a project in an IDE organizes source files and build settings so you can focus on code. In IntelliJ you typically choose New Project, select Java as the project type, and then pick a Project SDK — choose the JDK you installed. The IDE will create a source folder, usually named src, where you add Java classes. Use a clear package or simple default package for initial exercises. The advantage of using the IDE project is that it automatically compiles on run, manages the classpath, and links error diagnostics to the exact source line. A concrete example for this chapter: create a new project named MyFirstJavaProject, ensure the Project SDK points to your JDK, then add a new Java class named MyGreetingApp in src. When you run that class, IntelliJ compiles and executes it using the configured SDK. Beginners sometimes forget to set the Project SDK and wonder why the IDE uses a different Java version; always confirm the selected SDK in the project settings before running your first program. Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › IntelliJ Project
Quick steps
  1. Create New Project → select Java.
  2. Pick Project SDK: choose the installed JDK.
  3. Create project, then add a class inside src with a public class and main method.
Example

Project name: MyFirstJavaProject. Class: MyGreetingApp. Run action in the IDE compiles and executes using the selected SDK.

Common oversight
If the project SDK is unset or points to a different JDK, the IDE may compile with a different language level or runtime. Open Project Structure and confirm the SDK selection.

screens.title: Hello, World! — code explained
screens.narratorSegment: Now we examine the HelloWorld program line by line so the structure is clear. The file starts with a public class declaration using the class name that must match the filename. Inside, the entry point is the main method with the exact signature public static void main(String[] args). Public makes the method accessible to the JVM, static means it belongs to the class rather than an instance, void indicates no return value, and the String array parameter receives command-line arguments. Inside main, the statement uses the print stream to write text to the console. In the text example we print a greeting. A concrete example program shows these parts together. Beginners often make two errors: forgetting the semicolon at the end of a statement and changing the case of main, such as Main, which prevents the JVM from finding the entry point. screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often encounter a small set of recurring syntax and naming errors. One is the missing semicolon at the end of a statement. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome — in this lesson you will build the toolkit you need to write and run Java programs. We begin by installing a Java Development Kit, then configuring two system variables so the compiler and runtime are available from any terminal. You will learn the difference between the developer toolkit (the JDK), the runtime used to execute programs (the JRE), and the abstract executor that runs Java bytecode (the JVM). After verifying your installation, you'll set up a modern IDE so editing, compiling, and debugging are fast and visual. We will also write and run a simple greeting program both from the command line and inside the IDE, and highlight a few common mistakes that beginners make, such as missing semicolons and incorrect main signatures. By the end of this chapter you will have a working Java toolchain and a repeatable setup routine you can use on Windows or Mac O S. Think of this as preparing your developer kitchen: once your tools are organized, learning Object-Oriented Programming becomes practical and enjoyable. Ready to get your workspace ready?

By the end of this chapter you will confidently install the Java Development Kit and configure the environment so Java commands are available from your terminal. You will be able to explain the roles of the JDK, JRE, and JVM and why each matters when developing or running Java applications. You will set up a modern IDE—recommended is IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition—create a new Java project, select the correct project SDK, and understand how the IDE streamlines compilation and debugging. Finally, you will write, compile, and run a simple program both on the command line and inside the IDE, and you will know how to interpret and fix two common errors: a missing semicolon and an incorrect main method signature. Each objective combines a practical action and a reason why it helps your learning, so you leave with a repeatable routine rather than a one-off setup. These skills remove environment friction and let you focus on learning Java language features and object-oriented design.

These objectives pair action and verification so you can prove your setup works. First, after installing the JDK you will run two commands that validate both the runtime and the compiler. If both commands report the same JDK version, your PATH and JAVA_HOME are configured correctly. Second, you will open an IDE and confirm the Project SDK is the JDK you installed; this avoids mismatches between the command line and the IDE. Third, you will create a Java source file whose public class name matches the filename, compile it to bytecode, and run it. This process demonstrates the compile and run lifecycle and clarifies why the javac compiler produces. class files and the JVM executes those files. Finally, you will intentionally introduce two small errors — a missing semicolon and a wrong main signature — and use IDE hints and error messages to fix them. These checks teach you how to read compiler and runtime diagnostics, which is a critical debugging skill.

Let's make the trio of Java components clear and memorable. The Java Development Kit, or JDK, is the full developer toolkit: it contains the Java compiler, development tools, and the Java Runtime Environment. The JRE provides the environment to run Java applications; it bundles a JVM implementation and the core class libraries. The Java Virtual Machine is the abstract machine that executes Java bytecode and provides platform independence. A useful way to think about this is nested boxes: the JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM. When you develop code you need the JDK because only it includes the compiler that turns human-readable Java files into bytecode. If you only want to run already-compiled programs, the JRE is sufficient. An example: you write HelloWorld. java and run the compiler in the JDK to produce HelloWorld. class. That class file can be executed by any JVM on any platform. A common misconception is thinking the JVM compiles source code — it does not. Compilation is a separate step handled by the compiler in the JDK. Remember: compile with the JDK, run with a JVM inside the JRE. How does that separation affect where you install components on a shared machine?

Understanding the compile-and-run pipeline helps demystify what happens when you build and execute Java code. The process starts with a source file, typically named with a public class that matches the filename. You run the Java compiler, called javac, which reads. java files and produces. class files containing Java bytecode. Bytecode is not platform machine code; it is an intermediate representation that the JVM interprets or just-in-time compiles to native instructions. When you use the java command to run a program, the JVM loads the class files, verifies their structure, links necessary classes, and executes the entry point method. A concrete example: saving HelloWorld. java, running javac HelloWorld. java creates HelloWorld. class, and running java HelloWorld launches the JVM which looks for the main method and begins execution. A common error to watch for is a filename that does not match the public class name; the compiler will refuse to produce correct class files in that case. Another misconception is thinking java runs source files directly — it runs bytecode only. Keep this pipeline in mind when troubleshooting compilation or runtime failures.

Installing the Java Development Kit is straightforward, but there are choices to make. The chapter mentions two common distribution sources: vendor-provided builds and open-source builds. For development, pick the latest stable JDK that matches the course expectations. On Windows, run the installer and note the installation directory; on Mac O S, use the provided package installer and observe the Home path format. After installation, you must configure environment variables so commands work in new terminals. Setting JAVA_HOME to the JDK installation path and adding the JDK bin directory to PATH are the two essential steps. A concrete example: on Windows you might set JAVA_HOME to C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-17 and add %JAVA_HOME%\bin to PATH; on Mac O S you set JAVA_HOME to the JDK home folder and add its bin to PATH. A common misconception is that downloading the JDK is sufficient; without updating PATH or restarting the terminal, commands still won’t be found. Always open a fresh terminal after installation and verify with java -version and javac -version to confirm success. Beginners often encounter a small set of recurring syntax and naming errors. One is the missing semicolon at the end of a statement. The compiler will point to the line with a syntax error. Another is changing the main method name or capitalization — the JVM expects the exact signature public static void main(String[] args) and will refuse to run the class if it cannot find it. A third frequent issue is saving a public class under a different filename; Java requires the public class name and the filename to match exactly. IDEs make resolving these problems easier: they highlight missing punctuation, suggest fixes, and warn when the main signature is incorrect. The IDE also links run failures to source lines and can show the stack trace. A practical workflow is to attempt a run, observe the error message, follow the IDE's hint, and re-run. This quick-feedback loop helps you learn the language rules faster than repeatedly editing in a plain text editor and guessing the issue. Let's recap the essential points you will reuse throughout the course. The JDK is the developer toolkit and includes the compiler needed to create bytecode. The JRE is the runtime package that contains a JVM implementation and core libraries used to execute bytecode. The JVM is the abstract executor that runs the platform-independent bytecode on different systems. Configure JAVA_HOME to point to your JDK installation and add the JDK's bin directory to your PATH so the java and javac commands work in any terminal.
